draft.title: Aggravating and mitigating factors
card: When a court sentences an offender, it looks at the crime and at the person who committed it. Some facts push the sentence up. Others pull it down.
a fact that makes the offence more serious and can lead to a harsher sentence. Examples are using violence, a prior criminal record, and targeting a vulnerable victim.
a fact that lessens the offender's blame and can lead to a lighter sentence. Examples are genuine remorse, a guilty plea, and having no prior record.
The judge weighs all the factors in the case. The sentence must still stay within the limits the law sets for that offence.
draft.remember: Aggravating factors can raise a sentence. Mitigating factors can lower it.

a.q: Which of these is a mitigating factor at sentencing?
opts: The offender pleaded guilty and showed remorse
The offender has several earlier convictions
The offender used a weapon to hurt the victim
The offender chose a victim who was elderly
a.why: A guilty plea and remorse lessen the offender's blame, so they can lead to a lighter sentence. The other three make the offence more serious, so they are aggravating.
a.clue: Which fact would make a judge more lenient?

b.q: Dan is sentenced for breaking into a house in Orange. He has two earlier break-in convictions, but he pleaded guilty and apologised. How are these facts best described?
opts: The record is aggravating, the plea and apology mitigating
The record is mitigating, the plea and apology aggravating
All three are aggravating because they involve the offence
All three are mitigating because Dan admitted the crime
b.why: A prior record shows a pattern of offending, so it is aggravating. The guilty plea and apology show remorse, so they are mitigating. The judge weighs both sets of factors, so one kind does not cancel the other out.
b.clue: Sort each fact by whether it adds to or lessens Dan's blame.

a.best: The offender pleaded guilty and showed remorse

b.best: The record is aggravating, the plea and apology mitigating

problems.detail: The card defines a mitigating factor as one that 'lessens the offender's blame' and lists a guilty plea as an example. In NSW, the guilty plea discount mainly reflects the plea's practical value: it saves time and cost and spares witnesses (R v Thomson & Houlton; Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act). It does not reduce blame. The definition is too narrow and teaches a wrong reason for the guilty plea discount.

The card says an aggravating factor 'makes the offence more serious' and gives a prior record as an example. A prior record is listed as aggravating in s21A, but under Veen (No 2) it does not make the offence itself more serious. It mainly reduces the leniency the court can show. The wording slightly misstates how a prior record works.
Why (a) repeats the inaccurate idea that a guilty plea lessens the offender's blame.

The clue for b asks students to sort facts by whether they 'add to or lessen Dan's blame'. This carries the same simplification: a guilty plea is not mitigating because it lessens blame, and a prior record does not add to blame for this offence.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. However, the card and explanations say a guilty plea lessens blame and a prior record makes the offence more serious, which misstates NSW sentencing law. The definitions should be reworded, for example 'can make a lighter sentence appropriate' rather than 'lessens blame'.

proposal.title: Aggravating and mitigating factors
card: When sentencing, a judge looks at the offence and the offender. The judge weighs facts that push the sentence up against facts that pull it down, within the maximum penalty the law sets.
a fact that can lead to a harsher sentence. Using violence or targeting a vulnerable victim are examples, as they make the offence more serious.
a fact that can lead to a lighter sentence. Examples are genuine remorse, good character, having no prior record, and a guilty plea.

A prior record is aggravating because the court can show less leniency, not because this offence is worse. A guilty plea earns a discount mainly because it saves a trial and spares witnesses from giving evidence.
proposal.remember: Aggravating factors can raise a sentence. Mitigating factors, including a guilty plea, can lower it.

a.q: Why does a guilty plea usually lead to a lighter sentence?
opts: It saves a trial and spares witnesses from giving evidence
It proves the offender is less to blame for the crime
It shows the offence was less serious than first charged
It shows the offender has no earlier criminal record
a.why: A guilty plea has practical value: the court avoids a trial and witnesses do not have to give evidence. It does not change how much the offender is to blame, so the blame option is the tempting mistake.
a.clue: Think about what a trial costs the court and the people in it.

b.q: Dan is sentenced for breaking into a house in Orange. He has two earlier break-in convictions, but he pleaded guilty and apologised. How are these facts best described?
opts: The record is aggravating, the plea and apology mitigating
The record is mitigating, the plea and apology aggravating
All three are aggravating because they involve the offence
All three are mitigating because Dan admitted the crime
b.why: Dan's record is aggravating: it does not make this break-in worse, but the court can show him less leniency. His apology can show remorse and his plea saves a trial, so both are mitigating. Admitting the crime does not turn his record into a mitigating factor.
b.clue: Which facts could earn Dan a lighter sentence, and which could not?

a.best: It saves a trial and spares witnesses from giving evidence

b.best: The record is aggravating, the plea and apology mitigating
